thread.title: Apple Stock Deserves Another Look Because Cash Is High and Sentiment Is Low

title: Apple Stock Deserves Another Look Because Cash Is High and Sentiment Is Low
text:
You Should Look at Apple Because It Has Cash but Everyone Hates It By Jan. 27, 2019 7:00 a.m. Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Barron’s recently screened for stocks with low (or no) debt that can offer investors both: 1) safety in tougher economic times; and 2) potential for market-beating returns.
The idea for our screen bubbled up from conversations we had with portfolio managers. Earlier in the year we asked some pros about what they learned and lamented from the travails of 2018 .
Many said they wished they paid more attention to balance-sheet quality. Several investors felt burned by some investments with more debt that fell harder than the overall market when investor sentiment soured.
One stock came up again and again in our conversations–as an example of balance-sheet quality and as a potential pick for 2019–was Apple (AAPL) . Apple didn’t make the cut for the low-debt story. Instead, we went with KLA-Tencor (KLAC) , Gilead Sciences (GILD) , Gentex (GNTX) , and Teradyne (TER) . Four solid companies in their own right. Still, we thought Apple deserved honorable mention.
And Apple is truly the king of cash. Well, one of the kings of cash. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK. B) has more cash than Apple, but Berkshire is an insurance company and Warren Buffett deserves his own category.
Apple has $123 billion more cash than debt on its books. Still, the company’s fall from grace has been precipitous. Apple lost nearly 40% of its market value from Oct. 3 to Jan 3., when the stock hit its 52-week low. That’s $430 billion gone to money heaven. Apple stock hasn’t participated in the January rally, either. Apple shares are flat, and the S&P 500 has gained 6% year to date.
Today, Apple trades for about $157, or 12.6 times analysts’ estimates for calendar 2019 earnings. (Apple’s fiscal year actually ends in September.) That’s a 15% discount to its historical average.
It gets better–or cheaper: $123 billion in cash is about $26 per share. If you deduct that from the $157 stock price Apple shares trade for 10 times estimated earnings.
Does Apple deserve a higher multiple? Apple’s return on assets is in the top quartile among S&P 500 components, and the company has grown revenue and earnings by 7% and 13% a year on average, respectively, for the last three years.
Don’t forget that companies with less debt have traditionally been good bets. Our screens revealed companies with low debt (the lowest quintile for debt levels among S&P 500 components) have outperformed higher-debt firms (the top quintile) by about 1 percentage point a year for the last 25 years. That may not sound like much of an edge, but it amounts to about 30% more money compounded over that span. Low-debt stocks also have less volatility than the rest of the stock market on average.
More money with less risk shouldn’t be possible. You’re supposed to get more return for taking more risk. Low-debt stocks are the equivalent of an economic free lunch. Go figure.
We rechecked our numbers and scanned academic literature and found that our observation holds .
Another of the lessons Wall Street operators suggested at the beginning of the year was, “When the stock market roars, sell some more.” You can’t lose money taking a profit, after all. There is another saying on Wall Street. “When there’s blood in the streets, buy real estate.” So when sentiment gets too bearish, that can be a good time to buy. And now the time is ripe to revisit Apple fundamentals.
